# Problem 1: Giant kelp fronds

## a. Appropriate tests

The appropriate tests to determine the strength of the relationship between ocean temperature and giant kelp frond elongation rate are a Pearson correlation and a Spearman rank correlation. Pearson correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables (in this case, temperature and giant kelp frond elongation rate), while Spearman correlation measures the strength and direction of a relationship using ranked data rather than actual raw data values. A Spearman rank correlation is appropriate when assumptions of linearity or normality are not met.

## b. Creating a visualization 

```{r}
#| label: creating-visualization

# base layer ggplot with kelp_preds data frame
ggplot(data = kelp, 
       # setting aesthetics 
       mapping = aes(
         # x is temperature measured in celsius
         x = temp_c,
         # y is giant kelp frond elongation rate measured in cm per day
         y = kelp_elong)) +
  # first layer geom point showing individual data points
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen",
             # making points noticeably large
             size = 3) +
  # using labs to set axis titles
  labs(
    # x axis: ocean temperature
    x = "Ocean Temperature (°C)",
    # y axis: giant kelp frond elongation rate
    y = expression("Giant Kelp Frond Elongation Rate (" * cm ~ day^{-1} * ")"),
    # visualization title: finding from visualization
    title = "As ocean temperature increases, \nelongation rate decreases"
  ) +
  # setting a nice, basic theme
  theme_minimal()

```

## c. Checking assumptions and running a test

### Checking assumptions:

To check the assumptions for a Spearman rank correlation, we must test linearity and the normality of the two variables: temperature and giant kelp fond elongation rate.

To test for linearity, we are going to utilize the previously made correlation visualization (shown again for viewer convenience). 

```{r}
#| label: visualization-again
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# using previously made visualization to check for linearity 

# base layer ggplot with kelp_preds data frame
ggplot(data = kelp, 
       # setting aesthetics 
       mapping = aes(
         # x is temperature measured in celsius
         x = temp_c,
         # y is giant kelp frond elongation rate measured in cm per day
         y = kelp_elong)) +
  # first layer geom point showing individual data points
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen",
             # making points noticeably large
             size = 3) +
  # using labs to set axis titles
  labs(
    # x axis: ocean temperature
    x = "Ocean Temperature (°C)",
    # y axis: giant kelp frond elongation rate
    y = expression("Giant Kelp Frond Elongation Rate (" * cm ~ day^{-1} * ")"),
    # visualization title: finding from visualization
    title = "As ocean temperature increases, \nelongation rate decreases"
  ) +
  # setting a nice, basic theme
  theme_minimal()

```

Based on the orientation of the points, temperature and giant kelp frond elongation rate have a negative linear relationship. 

In order to test the normality of both variables, it is necessary to construct a QQ plot for each one.

QQ plot for temperature data normality:

```{r}
#| label: qq-temperature

# base layer ggplot with kelp data frame
ggplot(data = kelp,
       # sample temp_c variable because we are testing normality of temperature
       mapping = aes(sample = temp_c)) +
  # first layer individual data points in pretty turquoise color
  geom_qq(col = "turquoise") +
  # second layer is normality line in light green
  geom_qq_line(col = "lightgreen") +
  # relabeling axes
  labs(x = "Theoretical Quantiles", # x axis theoretical quantiles
       y = "Sample Quantiles", # y axis sample quantiles
       title = "Temperature (\u00B0C) normality") + #title is temperature normality
  # nice, minimal theme for aesthetics
  theme_minimal()

```

QQ plot for kelp elongation data normality:

```{r}
#| label: qq-kelp-elongation

# base layer ggplot with kelp data frame
ggplot(data = kelp,
       # sample is kelp elongation values because we are checking normality of kelp elongation
       mapping = aes(sample = kelp_elong)) +
  # first layer geom_qq shows individual data points in chartreuse
  geom_qq(col = "chartreuse2") +
  # second layer geom qq line shows normality line in dark green
  geom_qq_line(col = "darkgreen") +
  # labeling axes and title
  labs(x = "Theoretical Quantiles", # axis is theoretical quantiles
       y = "Sample Quantiles", # y is sample quantiles
       title = "Kelp elongation (cm/day) normality") + # title conveys that we are testing kelp elongation normality
  # nice, simple theme for aesthetics
  theme_minimal()

```

Based on the QQ plots above, the sample data points roughly align with the the reference line, so we can determine that both variables are normally distributed enough.

### Running tests:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# creating new object spearman_test from spearman rank test results
spearman_test <- cor.test(
  # first variable ocean temperature
  kelp$temp_c,
  # second variable giant kelp frond elongation rate
  kelp$kelp_elong,
  # running a spearman rank test to show correlation
  method = "spearman"
)

# display results
spearman_test

```


## d. Communicating results

To evaluate the strength of the relationship between temperature and giant kelp frond elongation rate, I used a Spearman rank correlation test because it can be used to measure the strength and direction of the correlation between two variables. After running this test, it has been concluded there is a moderate negative relationship between ocean temperature and giant kelp frond elongation rate. (Spearman rank correlation. test, $\rho$ = 0.68, S = 9216.1, p < 0.001, $\alpha$ = 0.05). 

Furthermore, according to our statistical test, ocean temperature does have an effect on giant kelp frond elongation rate, potentially because giant kelp may biologically thrive in particular ocean temperatures and conditions. This test suggests that they grow faster in colder temperatures. 

## e. Test implications

These results suggest that warmer ocean temperature (°C) could reduce giant kelp frond elongation rate (cm day$^{-1}$). Because giant kelp forests provide crucial habitat and food resources for marine animals, a slower growth rate of these giant kelp fronds could result in resource availability for the dependent species. As the ongoing climate crisis worsens, ocean temperatures are projected to continue rising, which can further encourage the slowing of giant kelp frond elongation. Furthermore, it is crucial to continue investing time and funding into developing solutions to rising sea temperatures.

## f. Double checking using a different test

```{r}
#| label: pearson-correlation-test

# pearson correlation test to assess strength and direction of relationship
cor.test(
  # first variable: temperature from kelp data frame
  kelp$temp_c,
  # second variable: elongation rate from kelp data frame
  kelp$kelp_elong,
  # specification that it is a pearson correlation test
  method = "pearson"
)

```

The Pearson correlation test and the Spearman rank correlation test produced the same overall conclusion: to reject the null hypothesis in favor of accepting the alternative hypothesis, as both tests found a statistically significant negative relationship between ocean temperature and giant kelp frond elongation rate.

The Pearson correlation measured the strength and direction of the relationship between temperature and kelp elongation rate (r = −0.68), and so did the Spearman test, yielding an almost exactly the same correlation coefficent ($\rho$ = -0.69).

# Problem 4: Statistical critique

## a. Revisiting and summarizing

For my statistical critique, I am examining a paper entitled, “Behavioural dynamics of water quality parameters and human exposure assessment of trace metals in Agulu Lake Water, South-East Nigeria” from the ScienceDirect journal. In this paper, they include a Spearman correlation, as they are focusing on examining relationships between pairs of variables. In
this scenario, the response variable could be one water quality parameter (like concentration of a specific trace metal) and the predictor variable could be another water quality parameter (like another trace metal).

```{r}
#| label: inserting-spearman-correlation-figure

# code to include png of the spearman correlation figure from paper
knitr::include_graphics(here("data", "spearman_screenshot copy.png"))
```

## b. Assessing visual clarity

I do think that the authors clearly represented their statistics in figures. Because they had so many trace metals (and relationships between these trace metals) to analyze, I believe this figure is an efficient way to visually demonstrate the correlation between two trace metals. This figure does not show explicit values per circle (Spearman correlation values), but the relative size of the circle compared to other sizes makes it easy to tell whether or not the presence of two trace metals are heavily related. The addition of the scale on the side also makes it very clear.

## c. Assessing aesthetic clarity

This figure is mostly ink, as they data is represented by purposefully sized dots. Given how many relationships between trace metals this figure is exploring, I feel as though they have excellent aesthetic clarity with minimal visual clutter. This figure shows 72 (half the figure is filled because the other half would be repetitive) relationships, so I commend them on their creative figure creation to convey so much data in one figure. 

## d. Recommendations

The only recommendation I would have for the authors is to add a title disclosing that the figure shows the correlation between the two types of trace metals found in the water. Although it is relatively clear that is the intended purpose of the figure in the caption, I think a title would serve this figure well because it is often the first component of a figure that a reader looks at is the title, and it lets them know what to expect while analyzing the figure. It is my understanding that a great figure is at least relatively clear to readers with just the title and figure itself.
